transaction_t6.definition: A transaction that undergoes a cascading rollback due to the failure of T 5.

transaction_t7.name: T 7
transaction_t7.definition: A transaction whose read(A) step is followed by the failure of T 5 leading to cascading rollback of T 6 and T 7.

transaction_t8.name: T 8
transaction_t8.definition: A transaction that reads multiple values and writes one value.

transaction_t9.name: T 9
transaction_t9.definition: A transaction that reads multiple values and displays their sum.

lock_a1_exclusive_mode.name: Lock a1 in Exclusive Mode
lock_a1_exclusive_mode.definition: A lock on a1 in exclusive mode required by the two-phase locking protocol for T 8.

i_th_cylinder.name: i-th Cylinder
i_th_cylinder.definition: The i-th tracks of all the platters together.

read_write_heads.name: Read-Write Heads
read_write_heads.definition: Components that keep the recording density high by being close to the disk surface.

head_crash.name: Head Crash
head_crash.definition: An event where the head contacts the disk surface, potentially scraping the recording medium off the disk.

dns_server.name: DNS Server
dns_server.definition: A server that stores information about names of computers and their associated IP addresses.

cs_dns_server.name: CS DNS Server
cs_dns_server.definition: A DNS server that stores information related to the Computer Science department.

math_dns_server.name: Math DNS Server
math_dns_server.definition: A DNS server that stores information related to the Mathematics department.

organization_data.name: Organization Data
organization_data.definition: Information about employees including identifiers, names, emails, departments, room numbers, phone numbers, and passwords.

crash_recovery_sub.name: Crash-Recovery Subsystem
crash_recovery_sub.definition: A subsystem responsible for managing recovery after a crash.

enterprise.name: Enterprise
enterprise.definition: An organization or business entity whose operations include the use of databases.

high_level_data.name: High-Level Data Model
high_level_data.definition: Provides a conceptual framework for specifying data requirements and structuring the database.

user_requirements.name: User Requirements
user_requirements.definition: A specification of what the database users need from the database.

replication_two_nodes.name: Replication to Two Nodes
replication_two_nodes.definition: Provides protection from data loss/unavailability in the event of single node failure.

replication_three_nodes.name: Replication to Three Nodes
replication_three_nodes.definition: Provides protection even in the event of two node failures.

low_cost_commodity_machines.name: Low-Cost Commodity Machines
low_cost_commodity_machines.definition: Typically used in systems that use three-way replication.

reliable_machines.name: Reliable Machines
reliable_machines.definition: Typically used in systems that use two-way replication.

rack_failure.name: Rack Failure
rack_failure.definition: Possible failure mode where all nodes in a rack fail due to issues like power supply or network switch failure.

single_node_failure.name: Single Node Failure
single_node_failure.definition: Most common failure mode where a single node in a parallel system fails.

random_merge.name: Random Merge
random_merge.definition: Merging data in the order received, which may be nondeterministic.

ordered_merge.name: Ordered Merge
ordered_merge.definition: Exploiting the sort order of input data to perform a more efficient merge.

local_sort_operation.name: Local Sort Operation
local_sort_operation.definition: Sorting data locally at each destination node.

parallel_external_sort_merge.name: Parallel External Sort-Merge
parallel_external_sort_merge.definition: An algorithm that involves local sorting at source nodes, followed by an exchange operation for range partitioning.

b_plus_tree_node_split.name: Node Split
b_plus_tree_node_split.definition: A node split occurs when a node in a B+ tree becomes too full.

b_plus_tree_fanout.name: Fanout
b_plus_tree_fanout.definition: Fanout refers to the maximum number of children a node in a B+ tree can have.

b_plus_tree_io_operation.name: I/O Operation
b_plus_tree_io_operation.definition: An I/O operation is a read or write operation performed on a storage device.

read_time_flash_storage.name: Read Time of Flash Storage
read_time_flash_storage.definition: A read of a 4 kilobyte page takes around 10 to 100 microseconds.

random_io_operation.name: Random I/O Operation
random_io_operation.definition: An operation to fetch any matching record.

composite_key.name: Composite Key
composite_key.definition: A key created by adding extra elements to an attribute that is not a candidate key.

performance_simulation.name: Performance-Simulation Model
performance_simulation.definition: A model used to test the performance of a database system before installation.

cpu_service.name: CPU Service
cpu_service.definition: A service in the performance-simulation model that represents the CPU.

disk_service.name: Disk Service
disk_service.definition: A service in the performance-simulation model that represents each disk.

buffer_service.name: Buffer Service
buffer_service.definition: A service in the performance-simulation model that represents the buffer.

concurrency_control_service.name: Concurrency Control Service
concurrency_control_service.definition: A service in the performance-simulation model that represents concurrency control.

ddl_interpreter.name: DDL Interpreter
ddl_interpreter.definition: Interprets DDL statements and records the definitions in the data dictionary.

dml_compiler.name: DML Compiler
dml_compiler.definition: Translates DML statements in a query language into an evaluation plan consisting of low-level instructions that the query-evaluation engine understands and performs query optimization.

query_evaluation_engine.name: Query Evaluation Engine
query_evaluation_engine.definition: Executes low-level instructions generated by the DML compiler.

granting_and_revoking_of_privileges.name: Granting and Revoking of Privileges
granting_and_revoking_of_privileges.definition: The process of assigning and removing permissions to users.

dean.name: Dean
dean.definition: A role assigned to a user who is the dean of the university.

department_chair.name: Department Chair
department_chair.definition: A role assigned to a user who is the chair of a department.

role.name: Role
role.definition: A predefined set of permissions assigned to a user.

multiple_links_between_nodes.name: Multiple Links Between Nodes
multiple_links_between_nodes.definition: A method to ensure nodes remain connected even if one link fails.

majority_node_protocol.name: Majority Node Protocol
majority_node_protocol.definition: A protocol that ensures a majority of nodes are written/read to maintain consistency.

failed_node_detection.name: Failed Node Detection
failed_node_detection.definition: The process of detecting failed nodes and removing them from the system in the background.

sql_query_example.name: SQL Query Example
sql_query_example.definition: A query that selects name and course_id from instructor and teaches tables where instructor.ID equals teaches.ID.

attribute_name_conflict.name: Attribute Name Conflict
attribute_name_conflict.definition: Two relations in the from clause may have attributes with the same name, causing duplication in the result.

arithmetic_expression_result.name: Arithmetic Expression Result
arithmetic_expression_result.definition: An attribute resulting from an arithmetic expression in the select clause does not have a name.

renaming_attributes.name: Renaming Attributes
renaming_attributes.definition: A way provided by SQL to change the attribute names in the result relation.

multiset_relational_algebra.name: Multiset Relational Algebra
multiset_relational_algebra.definition: A version of relational algebra that works on multisets, allowing duplicates in the output.

tablet_server_node.name: Tablet Server Node
tablet_server_node.definition: A node responsible for serving a tablet.

record_numbering.name: Record Numbering
record_numbering.definition: Records in a relation must be numbered sequentially, starting from 0.

income_level_attribute.name: Income Level Attribute
income_level_attribute.definition: An attribute in the instructor_info relation that categorizes income into 5 levels.

yahoo_message_bus.name: Yahoo Message Bus
yahoo_message_bus.definition: A service used for asynchronous replication in the PNUTS system.

schema_change.name: Schema Change
schema_change.definition: Changes such as adding or deleting attributes or constraints.

tuple_version_number.name: Tuple Version Number
tuple_version_number.definition: A version number kept with each tuple to track changes.

primary_or_unique_key_constraint.name: Primary or Unique Key Constraint
primary_or_unique_key_constraint.definition: A type of constraint that ensures no two tuples have the same ID value.

relation_snapshot.name: Relation Snapshot
relation_snapshot.definition: A snapshot of a relation used for online constraint addition.

log_of_updates.name: Log of Updates
log_of_updates.definition: A log of updates that occur after a relation snapshot is taken.

avg_aggregate_function.name: AVG Aggregate Function
avg_aggregate_function.definition: A function that calculates the average of a set of values.

sum_aggregate_value.name: Sum Aggregate Value
sum_aggregate_value.definition: The total sum of values in a group.

count_aggregate_value.name: Count Aggregate Value
count_aggregate_value.definition: The number of tuples in a group.

min_aggregate_function.name: MIN Aggregate Function
min_aggregate_function.definition: A function that finds the smallest value in a set of values.

max_aggregate_function.name: MAX Aggregate Function
max_aggregate_function.definition: A function that finds the largest value in a set of values.

group_key_g.name: Group Key G
group_key_g.definition: The key used to group tuples in a materialized view.

base_relation_r.name: Base Relation R
base_relation_r.definition: The original relation from which the materialized view is derived.

entity_relationship_design.name: Entity-Relationship Design
entity_relationship_design.definition: A method used to create a relational database design.

relation_schemas.name: Relation Schemas
relation_schemas.definition: Schemas generated directly from the Entity-Relationship design.

university_database_schema.name: University Database Schema
university_database_schema.definition: The database schema for the university example.

in_dep_relation.name: in_dep Relation
in_dep_relation.definition: A relation representing the result of a natural join on the relations corresponding to instructor and department.

multiset_semijoin_operator.name: Multiset Semijoin Operator
multiset_semijoin_operator.definition: Outputs the same tuples as the semijoin operator, but with the number of duplicates of each tuple r i in the semijoin result being the same as the number of duplicates of r i in r.

anti_semijoin_operator.name: Anti-Semijoin Operator
anti_semijoin_operator.definition: If a tuple r i appears n times in r, it appears n times in the result of r ⋉ θ s if there does not exist any tuple s j in s such that r i and s j satisfy predicate θ; otherwise r i does not appear in the result.

cascading_rollback.name: Cascading Rollback
cascading_rollback.definition: A situation where a single transaction failure leads to a series of transaction rollbacks.

cascadeless_schedule.name: Cascadeless Schedule
cascadeless_schedule.definition: A schedule where cascading rollbacks cannot occur.

database_performance_monitoring_tools.name: Database Performance Monitoring Tools
database_performance_monitoring_tools.definition: Tools provided by database systems to monitor database system performance.

pg_stat_statements.name: pg_stat_statements
pg_stat_statements.definition: A view relation in PostgreSQL used to monitor resource usage of SQL statements.

pgrowlocks.name: pgrowlocks
pgrowlocks.definition: A view relation in PostgreSQL used to monitor lock contention.

show_processinfo.name: SHOW PROCESSINFO
show_processinfo.definition: A command in MySQL used to monitor what transactions are currently executing and their resource usage.

sp_monitor.name: sp_monitor
sp_monitor.definition: A stored procedure in Microsoft SQL Server used to monitor system resource usage.

sp_who.name: sp_who
sp_who.definition: A stored procedure in Microsoft SQL Server used to monitor system resource usage.

sp_lock.name: sp_lock
sp_lock.definition: A stored procedure in Microsoft SQL Server used to monitor lock contention.

oracle_database_sql_tuning_guide.name: Oracle Database SQL Tuning Guide
oracle_database_sql_tuning_guide.definition: An online document providing details of similar views in Oracle.

redo_lsn.name: RedoLSN
redo_lsn.definition: A property set to the minimum of the RecLSNs of the pages in the DirtyPageTable.

transaction_end_log_record.name: Transaction End Log Record
transaction_end_log_record.definition: A log record indicating the end of a transaction.

cloud_service.name: Cloud Service Model
cloud_service.definition: A model for providing cloud-based services.

operating.name: Operating System
operating.definition: Software that manages computer hardware and software resources.

container.name: Container
container.definition: A lightweight, standalone executable package that includes everything needed to run an application.

ajax_url_load.name: ajax.url(url).load()
ajax_url_load.definition: A function that fetches JSON data from a web service URL and fills the rows of a table.

my_table.name: myTable
my_table.definition: A table whose rows are filled with JSON data fetched from a web service.

country_selection_form.name: form that allows you to select a country
country_selection_form.definition: A form that enables users to select a country from a list.

state_selection_dropdown.name: drop-down list of states
state_selection_dropdown.definition: A dropdown list that displays states from a selected country.

algorithm_for_3nf_decomposition.name: Algorithm for 3NF Decomposition
algorithm_for_3nf_decomposition.definition: An algorithm for finding a dependency-preserving, lossless decomposition into 3NF.

dept_advisor.name: dept_advisor
dept_advisor.definition: An example database schema from Section 7.3.2.

http_protocol.name: HTTP Protocol
http_protocol.definition: The protocol used to send a web service request.

rest.name: REST
rest.definition: A simpler approach to implementing web services where web service function calls are executed by a standard HTTP request to a URL at an application server.

url.name: URL
url.definition: A Uniform Resource Locator used in the REST approach to identify the location of the web service function.

xml.name: XML
xml.definition: An encoding used for the results of web service requests, seen earlier in Section 8.1.3.

map_interface.name: Map Interface
map_interface.definition: A graphical user interface that displays a map and can fetch new parts of the map using a RESTful interface.

recovery_in_main_memory_databases.name: Recovery in Main-Memory Databases
recovery_in_main_memory_databases.definition: Performing recovery in parallel using multiple cores to minimize recovery time.

non_volatile_ram.name: Non-Volatile RAM
non_volatile_ram.definition: A type of non-volatile storage system that supports direct access to individual words.

storage_class_memory.name: Storage Class Memory (SCM)
storage_class_memory.definition: A type of non-volatile RAM that supports very fast random access.

redo_logging.name: Redo Logging
redo_logging.definition: A technique used in database recovery to ensure that all committed transactions are written to the log file.

undo_logging.name: Undo Logging
undo_logging.definition: A technique used in database recovery to reverse the effects of uncommitted transactions.

single_lock_manager.name: Single Lock-Manager Approach
single_lock_manager.definition: A method where the system maintains a single lock manager in a chosen node for handling all lock and unlock requests.

single_scan.name: Single Scan
single_scan.definition: A process of reading through a database table or index once to retrieve data.

round_of_communication.name: Round of Communication
round_of_communication.definition: A single exchange of data between a client and a server.

schema_evolution.name: Schema Evolution
schema_evolution.definition: The process of changing the structure of a database schema over time to meet evolving organizational needs.

fundamental_constraint.name: Fundamental Constraint
fundamental_constraint.definition: A constraint that is expected to remain unchanged over time.

expected_change.name: Expected Change
expected_change.definition: A constraint that is anticipated to change in the future.

concurrency_control_policy.name: Concurrency Control Policy
concurrency_control_policy.definition: A set of rules used to ensure that multiple transactions can be executed concurrently without generating unacceptable schedules.

trivial_example_locking_policy.name: Trivial Example Locking Policy
trivial_example_locking_policy.definition: A policy where a transaction acquires a lock on the entire database before starting and releases it after committing.

multiversion_two_phase_locking.name: Multiversion Two-Phase Locking
multiversion_two_phase_locking.definition: A method used in database systems where read-only transactions see the old value of ts-counter until T i has successfully committed.

mediator_systems.name: Mediator Systems
mediator_systems.definition: Systems that support a common schema and queries, but not updates, against the schema.

data_virtualization.name: Data Virtualization
data_virtualization.definition: An approach that allows applications to access data from multiple databases/data sources without enforcing a common schema.

external_data.name: External Data
external_data.definition: Data stored in external sources that can be accessed from a database.

foreign_tables.name: Foreign Tables
foreign_tables.definition: Views defined in a database whose actual data are stored in an external data source.

bcnf_relation.name: BCNF Relation
bcnf_relation.definition: A relation that satisfies the BCNF condition.

exclusive_mode_lock.name: Exclusive Mode Lock
exclusive_mode_lock.definition: A type of lock that prevents any other transaction from accessing the locked resource in any mode.

shared_mode_lock.name: Shared Mode Lock
shared_mode_lock.definition: A type of lock that allows multiple transactions to read the locked resource but prevents any transaction from modifying it.

transaction_t4.name: Transaction T4
transaction_t4.definition: A transaction holding a shared-mode lock on A and requesting an exclusive-mode lock on B.

multiversion_two_phase_locking_protocol.name: Multiversion Two-Phase Locking Protocol
multiversion_two_phase_locking_protocol.definition: A protocol that combines the advantages of multiversion concurrency control with the advantages of two-phase locking.

ts_counter.name: TS Counter
ts_counter.definition: A counter that is incremented during commit processing and used as a timestamp for each version of a data item.

view_definitions.name: View Definitions
view_definitions.definition: Descriptions used to provide a global view of data stored in local databases.

forced_output_of_block.name: Forced Output of a Block
forced_output_of_block.definition: A write to disk to ensure certain data on disk are in a consistent state.

logging_mechanism.name: Logging Mechanism
logging_mechanism.definition: A mechanism used in conjunction with forced output to ensure transaction updates are not lost.

read_write_contention.name: Read-Write Contention
read_write_contention.definition: A situation where read and write transactions compete for access to the same data.

write_write_contention.name: Write-Write Contention
write_write_contention.definition: A situation where multiple write transactions compete for access to the same data.

prior_knowledge.name: Prior Knowledge Model
prior_knowledge.definition: A model that requires prior knowledge about the order in which the database items will be accessed.

partial_ordering.name: Partial Ordering
partial_ordering.definition: A model that imposes a partial ordering on the set of all data items, where d_i → d_j means any transaction accessing both d_i and d_j must access d_i before d_j.

rooted_tree.name: Rooted Tree
rooted_tree.definition: A type of graph used in this section for simplicity, where the set D is viewed as a directed acyclic graph.

alphabetically_smallest_relation.name: Alphabetically Smallest Relation
alphabetically_smallest_relation.definition: The relation with the lexicographically smallest name in a set of relations.

division.name: Division
division.definition: A step in the join-order selection process where a set of relations is divided into subsets.

blockchain_transaction.name: Blockchain Transaction
blockchain_transaction.definition: A transaction that may include executable code.

turing_complete_language.name: Turing-Complete Language
turing_complete_language.definition: A language that can express all possible computations.

database_buffers.name: Database Buffers
database_buffers.definition: Allow writes to be performed in-memory and output to disk at a later time.

metadata.name: Metadata
metadata.definition: Data that provides information about other data.

abstract_view.name: Abstract View
abstract_view.definition: An approach where the system hides certain details of how the data are stored and maintained.

conflict_equivalence.name: Conflict Equivalence
conflict_equivalence.definition: A relationship between schedules where one schedule can be transformed into another without changing the outcome.

schedule_3.name: Schedule 3
schedule_3.definition: A schedule that is conflict serializable as it is conflict equivalent to the serial schedule 1.

schedule_7.name: Schedule 7
schedule_7.definition: A schedule that is not conflict serializable as it is not equivalent to the serial schedules <T 3, T 4> or <T 4, T 3>.

storage_manager.name: Storage Manager
storage_manager.definition: Important because databases typically require a large amount of storage space.

query_processor.name: Query Processor
query_processor.definition: Important because it helps the database system to simplify and facilitate access to data.

transaction_management_component.name: Transaction Management Component
transaction_management_component.definition: Part of the functional components of a database system.

disk_storage.name: Disk Storage
disk_storage.definition: Used for storing data when the main memory cannot hold all the information.

solid_state_disks.name: Solid-State Disks (SSDs)
solid_state_disks.definition: Faster than traditional disks but more costly, increasingly used for database storage.

gigabyte.name: Gigabyte
gigabyte.definition: Approximately 1 billion bytes, or 1000 megabytes (more precisely, 1024 megabytes).

terabyte.name: Terabyte
terabyte.definition: Approximately 1 trillion bytes or 1 million megabytes (more precisely, 1024 gigabytes).

exists_construct.name: Exists Construct
exists_construct.definition: Returns true if the argument subquery is nonempty.

correlated_subquery.name: Correlated Subquery
correlated_subquery.definition: A subquery that uses a correlation name from an outer query.

phase_1b.name: Phase 1b
phase_1b.definition: A phase in the Paxos Consensus Protocol where acceptors check their responses and respond with the highest accepted proposal number and value.

phase_2a.name: Phase 2a
phase_2a.definition: A phase in the Paxos Consensus Protocol where the proposer selects a value based on the responses from the acceptors.

accept_request.name: Accept Request
accept_request.definition: A message sent by a proposer to an acceptor during the Paxos Consensus Protocol.

phase_2b.name: Phase 2b
phase_2b.definition: A phase in the Paxos Consensus Protocol where acceptors decide whether to accept a proposed value.

support_vector_machine_classifier.name: Support Vector Machine Classifier
support_vector_machine_classifier.definition: A type of classifier that has been found to give very accurate classification across a range of applications.

class_a.name: Class A
class_a.definition: A class of points in a two-dimensional plane.

class_b.name: Class B
class_b.definition: Another class of points in a two-dimensional plane.

index_on_one_attribute.name: Index on One Attribute
index_on_one_attribute.definition: An index created on a single attribute of a relation.

hdfs_distributed_file.name: HDFS Distributed File System
hdfs_distributed_file.definition: A distributed file system that can be connected to the local file system of a machine.

local_file.name: Local File System
local_file.definition: The file system of a machine that can access files in HDFS.

namenode_machine.name: NameNode Machine
namenode_machine.definition: The machine that runs the NameNode, a critical component of HDFS.

free_space.name: Free Space
free_space.definition: Contiguous space between the final entry in the header array and the first record.

header_array.name: Header Array
header_array.definition: An array used to store information about records in a block.

end_of_free_space_pointer.name: End-of-Free-Space Pointer
end_of_free_space_pointer.definition: A pointer indicating the end of the free space in the block.

synchronous_replication.name: Synchronous Replication
synchronous_replication.definition: A method of database replication where updates are propagated to other replicas as part of a single transaction.

lazy_propagation.name: Lazy Propagation
lazy_propagation.definition: The practice of propagating updates to replicas after the transaction has committed at the primary node.

mesi_protocol.name: MESI Protocol
mesi_protocol.definition: A widely used protocol for managing cache coherence in shared-memory systems.

view.name: View
view.definition: A defined perspective of the database that hides details of the logical level and provides security mechanisms.

geographic_database.name: Geographic Database
geographic_database.definition: A database containing information about geographical areas.

online_map_and_navigation_service.name: Online Map and Navigation Service
online_map_and_navigation_service.definition: A service providing maps and navigation information over the internet.

distribution_network_information.name: Distribution-Network Information
distribution_network_information.definition: Information related to the network of cables and pipes used by public-service utilities.

land_usage_information.name: Land-Usage Information
land_usage_information.definition: Information about how land is being used, relevant for ecologists and planners.

ecologist.name: Ecologist
ecologist.definition: A scientist who studies ecosystems and their interactions.

planner.name: Planner
planner.definition: A professional who plans and designs urban and regional development.

land_record.name: Land Record
land_record.definition: A record of information about land ownership.

public_utility.name: Public Utility
public_utility.definition: An organization responsible for providing essential services like electricity, water, and telecommunications.

gps.name: GPS
gps.definition: Global Positioning System, a satellite-based navigation system.

shadow_copying.name: Shadow Copying
shadow_copying.definition: An alternative technique used by text editors but not in database systems.

sql_authorization.name: SQL Authorization Model
sql_authorization.definition: A component of the SQL standard that supports a flexible system of authorization based on roles.

user_id.name: User ID
user_id.definition: An identifier of the application user on whose behalf a query is being executed.

insert_privilege.name: Insert Privilege
insert_privilege.definition: A privilege that allows inserting into a relation with specified attributes.

public_user.name: Public User
public_user.definition: A special user name that refers to all current and future users of the system.

revoke_statement.name: Revoke Statement
revoke_statement.definition: A SQL statement used to revoke privileges from a user or role.

relation_instructor.name: Instructor Relation
relation_instructor.definition: A relation with attributes like ID and name.

in_clause.name: In Clause
in_clause.definition: A clause used in a SQL query to specify multiple values.

exists_clause.name: Exists Clause
exists_clause.definition: A clause used in a SQL query to check if any rows match a specified condition.

decorrelation_process.name: Decorrelation Process
decorrelation_process.definition: The process of replacing a nested query by a query with a join, semijoin, or antisemijoin.

aggregation_without_group_by.name: Aggregation Without Group By
aggregation_without_group_by.definition: A type of aggregation in a subquery where the results are aggregated without specifying a GROUP BY clause.

teaches_table.name: Teaches Table
teaches_table.definition: A table containing information about instructors teaching course sections.

ordered_indexing_techniques.name: Ordered Indexing Techniques
ordered_indexing_techniques.definition: Several techniques for ordered indexing, none of which is universally the best.

access_types.name: Access Types
access_types.definition: The types of access that are supported efficiently, such as finding records with a specified attribute value and finding records whose attribute values fall in a specified range.

access_time.name: Access Time
access_time.definition: The time it takes to find a particular data item, or set of items, using the technique in question.

insertion_time.name: Insertion Time
insertion_time.definition: The time it takes to insert a new data item, including the time to find the correct place to insert the new data item and update the index structure.

deletion_time.name: Deletion Time
deletion_time.definition: The time it takes to delete a data item, including the time to find the item to be deleted and update the index structure.

space_overhead.name: Space Overhead
space_overhead.definition: The additional space occupied by an index structure.

hashing.name: Hashing
hashing.definition: A widely used technique for building indices in main memory.

disk_based_hash_index.name: Disk-Based Hash Index
disk_based_hash_index.definition: A disk-based hash index where each bucket is a linked list of disk blocks.

lock_caching.name: Lock Caching
lock_caching.definition: A method where locks can be cached at the client machine to avoid communication with the server.

server.name: Server
server.definition: A component that provides data and handles lock requests.

cache.name: Cache
cache.definition: A local storage mechanism used to store frequently accessed data to reduce communication with the server.

instructor_tuple.name: Instructor Tuple
instructor_tuple.definition: A record in the instructors table.

department_total_salary.name: Department Total Salary
department_total_salary.definition: A view giving the total salary in each department.

static_partitioning.name: Static Partitioning
static_partitioning.definition: A method where the partitioning is decided at some point and is not automatically updated.

recomputation_of_partition_vectors.name: Recomputation of Partition Vectors
recomputation_of_partition_vectors.definition: The process of recalculating the partitioning vectors.

dynamic_techniques_for_avoiding_skew.name: Dynamic Techniques for Avoiding Skew
dynamic_techniques_for_avoiding_skew.definition: Techniques that can adapt continuously and less disruptively to avoid skew.

data_type_mismatch.name: Data Type Mismatch
data_type_mismatch.definition: The issue where data types used in one system are not supported by other systems, leading to potential translation complexities.

physical_representation_differences.name: Physical Representation Differences
physical_representation_differences.definition: Differences in how data is physically represented across systems, such as using 8-bit ASCII vs 16-bit Unicode, or varying floating-point and integer representations.

semantic_level_conversion.name: Semantic Level Conversion
semantic_level_conversion.definition: The process of converting data values to a common representation at the semantic level during integration, especially when dealing with units like inches and millimeters.

globally_unique_naming.name: Globally Unique Naming System

geo_names_database.name: GeoNames Database
geo_names_database.definition: A database providing unique names for geographical entities, which can help in resolving naming inconsistencies.

comparison_condition.name: Comparison Condition

node_n3.name: Node N3

aba_problem.definition: A problem that occurs when a process reads a node before another process deletes it and reinserts it, leading to an inconsistent state.

counter.name: Counter
counter.definition: A property that is incremented every time a pointer is updated and used alongside the pointer in the CAS instruction.

prevent_web_site_attacks.name: Prevent Web Site from Being Used to Launch XSS or XSRF Attacks
prevent_web_site_attacks.definition: Protect against XSS or XSRF attacks by disallowing HTML tags in user input.

disallow_html_tags.name: Disallow HTML Tags
disallow_html_tags.definition: Simplest technique to prevent XSS or XSRF attacks by disallowing HTML tags in user input.

functions_detect_strip_tags.name: Functions that Detect or Strip Tags
functions_detect_strip_tags.definition: Functions used to detect or remove HTML tags and scripts from user input.

parse_text_limit_constructs.name: Parse Text and Allow Limited HTML Constructs
parse_text_limit_constructs.definition: Functions that parse text and allow limited HTML constructs while disallowing dangerous ones.

protect_web_site_other_sites.name: Protect Web Site from XSS or XSRF Attacks Launched from Other Sites
protect_web_site_other_sites.definition: Steps to minimize risk when a user visits a different web site vulnerable to XSS.

http_protocol_check_referer.name: HTTP Protocol Check Referer

procedural_dml.name: Procedural DML

declarative_dml.name: Declarative DML

dense_nonclustering_index.definition: A type of dense index where the index stores a list of pointers to all records with the same search-key value.

seven_minute_rule.name: Seven Minute Rule
seven_minute_rule.definition: Data should be cached in memory if it is accessed more frequently than once in 7 minutes.

two_point_five_minute_rule.definition: Sequentially accessed data on hard disk should be cached in memory if they are used at least once in 2.5 minutes.

one_point_six_second_rule.definition: There is little benefit in caching sequentially accessed data in memory if the access frequency is less than once every 1.6 seconds.

line_segment.name: Line Segment

polyline.name: Polyline

arbitrary_curve.name: Arbitrary Curve

polygon.name: Polygon
polygon.definition: A polygon can be represented by listing its vertices in order, as in Figure 8.5.

triangulation.name: Triangulation

double_line_constraint.name: Double Line Constraint

student_dept.name: Student-Department Relationship

dept_year_relation.name: dept_year relation
dept_year_relation.definition: A relation with one column for each value of an attribute.

sql_features.name: SQL features

employee_data.name: Employee Data

authentication_information.name: Authentication Information

user_category.name: User Category

authorization_information.name: Authorization Information

web_browser_directory.name: Web Browser Directory

central_authentication_service.name: Central Authentication Service

single_sign_on.name: Single Sign-On System

kerberos.name: Kerberos

security_assertion_markup_language.name: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)
security_assertion_markup_language.definition: A language used for exchanging security information, particularly in web applications.

resource_description_format.name: Resource Description Format (RDF)
resource_description_format.definition: A data representation that has found wide acceptance for representing extremely large knowledge bases.

triple.name: Triple

parallel_evaluation_plan.name: Parallel Evaluation Plan

sequential_evaluation_plan.name: Sequential Evaluation Plan

basic_sequential_cost.name: Basic Sequential Cost Model

simple_cost.name: Simple Cost Model

partitioning_techniques.name: Partitioning Techniques

scheduling_operators.name: Scheduling Operators
scheduling_operators.definition: The process of determining the order in which operators are executed.

profile_data.name: User Profile

bigtable_data.name: Bigtable Data Model
bigtable_data.definition: A custom model for storing complex data, including support for records with many optional columns.

probabilistic_data.name: Probabilistic Data Structure
probabilistic_data.definition: A data structure used to compute an efficient overapproximation of the semijoin result.

partitioning_relations_vertically.name: Partitioning Relations Vertically
partitioning_relations_vertically.definition: The process of splitting a relation into multiple relations based on certain attributes.

course_credit_relation.name: Course Credit Relation

course_title_dept_relation.name: Course Title and Department Relation
course_title_dept_relation.definition: A relation with the schema: course_title_dept ( course_id, title, dept_name ).

operating_system_files.name: Operating System Files
operating_system_files.definition: A method to store information on a computer.

application_programs.name: Application Programs

new_major.name: New Major

permanent_files.name: Permanent Files
permanent_files.definition: Files used to record information about instructors, students, course offerings, and other details.

conventional_operating.name: Conventional Operating System
conventional_operating.definition: A system that supports the typical file-processing system.

join_cost_formulae.name: Join Cost Formulae
join_cost_formulae.definition: Formulae used to calculate the cost of joining relations.

file_number.name: File Number

prereq_relation.name: prereq Relation

cs_347_course.name: CS-347 Course

cs_315_course.definition: A course that is a prerequisite for CS-319.

cs_190_course.name: CS-190 Course
cs_190_course.definition: A course that is a prerequisite for CS-315.

cache_miss.name: Cache Miss
cache_miss.definition: An event where data is not found in the cache.

memory_resident_data.name: Memory-Resident Data
memory_resident_data.definition: Data that is stored in the main memory of a computer system.

multiple_threads.name: Multiple Threads

parallel_query_processing.name: Parallel Query Processing Algorithm
parallel_query_processing.definition: An algorithm that processes queries using multiple threads on a single CPU core.

transaction_t26.name: Transaction T26

schedule_6.name: Schedule 6
schedule_6.definition: A specific schedule mentioned in the context.

figure_18_19.name: Figure 18.19
figure_18_19.definition: A figure referenced in the context.

paxos_group.name: Paxos Group
paxos_group.definition: A set of replicas for a particular partition in distributed systems.

get_operation.name: Get Operation

cost_based_query_optimizer.name: Cost-Based Query Optimizer
cost_based_query_optimizer.definition: A type of query optimizer that computes the cost of each alternative and picks the least cost alternative.

expression.name: Expression

cost.name: Cost

statistics.name: Statistics
statistics.definition: Data used to estimate the cost of executing an expression.

data_storage_and_definition_language.name: Data Storage and Definition Language
data_storage_and_definition_language.definition: A special type of DDL used to specify the storage structure and access methods used by the database system.

consistency_constraints.name: Consistency Constraints
consistency_constraints.definition: Constraints that ensure data values stored in the database satisfy certain conditions.

domain_constraints.name: Domain Constraints
domain_constraints.definition: Constraints that restrict the values an attribute can take to a specific domain.

postgres_serial_type.name: PostgreSQL Serial Type
postgres_serial_type.definition: A PostgreSQL data type that provides the same effect as a serial number.

sequence_number_acquisition.name: Sequence Number Acquisition

transaction_abortion.name: Transaction Abortion
transaction_abortion.definition: The event where a transaction is terminated without committing its changes.

tuple_identifier_value.name: Tuple Identifier Value
tuple_identifier_value.definition: The unique identifier value assigned to a tuple in the database.

database_sequence_counter.name: Database Sequence Counter
database_sequence_counter.definition: A sequence counter stored in normal tuples, locked in a two-phase manner.

catalog.name: Catalog

java_sql_interface.name: Java SQL Interface
java_sql_interface.definition: An interface that contains the interface definitions for the functionality provided by JDBC.

random_write_performance_issue.name: Random Write Performance Issue
random_write_performance_issue.definition: Performance degradation due to random writes in the B+ tree index structure.

buffer_size.name: Buffer Size
buffer_size.definition: The amount of memory allocated for caching data.

flash_based_ssd.name: Flash-Based SSD
flash_based_ssd.definition: A type of storage device that is faster for random I/O but still incurs costs for page writes.

query_optimizer_parallel.name: Query Optimizer for Parallel Execution
query_optimizer_parallel.definition: A component used in optimizing queries for parallel execution.

query_optimizer_sequential.name: Query Optimizer for Sequential Execution
query_optimizer_sequential.definition: A component used in optimizing queries for sequential execution.

plan_alternatives.name: Plan Alternatives
plan_alternatives.definition: Different possible execution plans for a query.

partitioning_schemes.name: Partitioning Schemes
partitioning_schemes.definition: Different ways of dividing input and intermediate results in a parallel setting.

cost_models.name: Cost Models
cost_models.definition: Models used to estimate the cost of executing a query.

join_r1_r2.name: r1 ⋈ r2
join_r1_r2.definition: A join operation between relations r1 and r2.

join_r3_r4.name: r3 ⋈ r4
join_r3_r4.definition: A join operation between relations r3 and r4.

intermediate_result_t1.definition: An intermediate result of the join operation r1 ⋈ r2.

intermediate_result_t2.name: t2
intermediate_result_t2.definition: An intermediate result of the join operation r3 ⋈ r4.

sigma_a_leq_v_r.name: σ A ≤ v ( r )
sigma_a_leq_v_r.definition: A selection of the form σ A ≤ v ( r ) where A is an attribute and v is a value.

min_a_r.name: min( A, r )

max_a_r.name: max( A, r )
max_a_r.definition: The maximum value of attribute A in relation r.

histogram_a.definition: A histogram on attribute A that provides a more accurate estimate of the number of records satisfying the condition A ≤ v.

computation_and_maintenance_of_statistic.name: computing and maintaining statistics
computation_and_maintenance_of_statistic.definition: The process of computing and maintaining statistics on relations.

sample_of_underlying_data.name: sample of the underlying data
sample_of_underlying_data.definition: Statistics are often computed from a sample of the underlying data, instead of examining the entire collection of data.

manual_choice.name: Manual Choice

workload.name: Workload
workload.definition: The set of queries used to measure the performance of materialized views.

parallel_query_execution.name: Parallel Query Execution Model
parallel_query_execution.definition: A model that breaks parallel query processing into partitioning of data and execution of operations on local data.

sort_operation.name: Sort Operation

interoperation_parallelism.name: Interoperation Parallelism
interoperation_parallelism.definition: Parallelizing the execution of different operators of a query.

hash_map_data.name: Hash Map Data Structure

memcached.name: Memcached

database_query.name: Database Query
database_query.definition: A process that retrieves data from a database based on a specified key.

user_data.name: User Data
user_data.definition: Data related to users, such as information stored in a database.

memcached_instance.name: Memcached Instance
memcached_instance.definition: An instance of the memcached caching system that can store and retrieve data from multiple machines.

block_level_partitioning.name: Block-Level Partitioning
block_level_partitioning.definition: A technique supported by RAID systems that does not offer control over which tuples of a relation are stored on which disk or node.

tuple_level_partitioning.name: Tuple-Level Partitioning
tuple_level_partitioning.definition: A partitioning strategy used in parallel database systems where data is partitioned at the level of tuples.

vertical_partitioning.name: Vertical Partitioning
vertical_partitioning.definition: A partitioning strategy where a relation is divided into smaller relations based on columns.

big_data_systems.name: Big Data Systems
big_data_systems.definition: Systems developed over the past decade for storing and processing Big Data using large clusters of machines.

recursive_query.name: Recursive Query
recursive_query.definition: A type of query that may be computed using iterative techniques or other efficient methods.

monotonic.name: Monotonic
monotonic.definition: A property of recursive queries where adding more tuples to the view relation does not reduce the result of the query.

view_relation_instance_v1.name: View Relation Instance V1
view_relation_instance_v1.definition: An instance of a view relation in the context of recursive queries.

view_relation_instance_v2.name: View Relation Instance V2
view_relation_instance_v2.definition: Another instance of a view relation in the context of recursive queries.

function_findallprereqs.name: Function findAllPrereqs
function_findallprereqs.definition: A function that computes the result of a recursive query using an efficient method.

password_based_authentication.name: Password-Based Authentication
password_based_authentication.definition: A method used by operating systems and database systems for user verification.

challenge_response.name: Challenge-Response System

metadata_from_communication_networks.name: Metadata from Communication Networks
metadata_from_communication_networks.definition: Data from communication networks, including traffic and other monitoring information for data networks, and call information for voice networks.

call_information_for_voice_networks.name: Call Information for Voice Networks
call_information_for_voice_networks.definition: Information about calls made on voice networks.

web_search_histories_annotated_with_user.name: Web Search Histories Annotated with User Profile Information
web_search_histories_annotated_with_user.definition: Search histories of users annotated with their profile information.

social_media_data.name: Social Media Data
social_media_data.definition: Data from social media platforms used for making business decisions.

input_validation.name: Input Validation
input_validation.definition: Functions written in JavaScript can be used to perform error checks on user input.

html5_input_tag.name: HTML5 Input Tag
html5_input_tag.definition: An HTML tag that allows specifying validation constraints directly.

javascript_function.name: JavaScript Function
javascript_function.definition: A function written in JavaScript that performs validation checks.

form_submission.name: Form Submission
form_submission.definition: The process of submitting a form to the server.

alert_box.name: Alert Box
alert_box.definition: A dialog box that appears to show messages to the user.

crop_insurance_smart_contract.name: Crop Insurance Smart Contract
crop_insurance_smart_contract.definition: A specific type of smart contract that pays a farmer based on rainfall during the growing season.

alternative_notations_for_modeling_data.name: Alternative Notations for Modeling Data
alternative_notations_for_modeling_data.definition: Different ways to represent data models in design tools.

entity_view.name: Entity View
entity_view.definition: A representation of an entity without its attributes.

relational_view.name: Relational View
relational_view.definition: A representation of an entity with its attributes.

tf_idf.name: TF-IDF Approach
tf_idf.definition: Using term frequency and inverse document frequency as a measure of the relevance of a document.

inverse_document_frequency.name: Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)

term_frequency.name: Term Frequency (TF)

weight.name: Weight

attribute_name_prefixing.definition: Prefixing the name of the relation from which the attribute originally came before the attribute name.

differential.name: Differential
differential.definition: Changes (inserts and deletes) to a relation or expression.

hash_structure_after_six_insertions.name: Hash Structure After Six Insertions
hash_structure_after_six_insertions.definition: A hash structure after six insertions.

hash_structure_after_seven_insertions.name: Hash Structure After Seven Insertions
hash_structure_after_seven_insertions.definition: A hash structure after seven insertions.

hash_structure_after_eleven_insertions.name: Hash Structure After Eleven Insertions
hash_structure_after_eleven_insertions.definition: A hash structure after eleven insertions.

simple_descriptive_attribute.name: Simple Descriptive Attribute
simple_descriptive_attribute.definition: An attribute that does not have any complex relationships or dependencies.

er.name: E-R Model

general_purpose_programming_language.name: General-Purpose Programming Language
general_purpose_programming_language.definition: A language used for non-declarative tasks like printing reports, interacting with users, or sending results to GUIs.

diagrammatic_representation.name: Diagrammatic Representation

e_r_diagram_notation.name: E-R Diagram Notation
e_r_diagram_notation.definition: There is no universal standard for E-R diagram notation, and different books and E-R diagram software use different notations.

goal_high_availability.name: High Availability
goal_high_availability.definition: The database must function almost all the time.

robustness.name: Robustness
robustness.definition: The ability of a distributed system to continue functioning even during failures.

aggregate_function_count.name: Count
aggregate_function_count.definition: A function used to count the number of tuples in a relation.

sql_count_notation.name: SQL Count Notation
sql_count_notation.definition: The notation in SQL for the count function, which is count(*)

election_of_coordinator.name: Election of Coordinator
election_of_coordinator.definition: A process used to select a coordinator when votes may be split.

bully.name: Bully Algorithm
bully.definition: An algorithm for election based on the idea that the highest-numbered candidate will win the election.

round_number.name: Round Number

candidate_node.name: Candidate Node
candidate_node.definition: A node that proposes itself as a candidate in the election.

partitioned.name: Partitioned System

update_protocol.name: Update Protocol
update_protocol.definition: A protocol for handling updates in a distributed system.

write_all_available_protocol.name: Write-All-Available Protocol
write_all_available_protocol.definition: A protocol that allows updates on all available replicas.

basically_available.name: Basically Available
basically_available.definition: A property of a system where updates are allowed even in the presence of failures.

soft_state.name: Soft State
soft_state.definition: A property of a system where the state of the database may not be precisely defined.

eventually_consistent.name: Eventually Consistent
eventually_consistent.definition: A property of a system where the state of the database will eventually match the latest state.

sec_time_slot_relationship_set.name: Sec-Time Slot Relationship Set

gender_value_f.name: Gender Value F

distributed_transaction.name: Distributed Transaction System
distributed_transaction.definition: A system structure with multiple nodes, each of which can fail independently.

shared_memory_parallel_database.name: Shared-Memory Parallel Database System
shared_memory_parallel_database.definition: A type of parallel database system where components do not have independent modes of failure.

sorted_partitions.name: Sorted Partitions
sorted_partitions.definition: Partitions of data that have been sorted at each node.

salary_field.name: Salary Field
salary_field.definition: A column in the instructor relation that stores the salary of each instructor.

select_statement.name: Select Statement
select_statement.definition: A SQL command used to retrieve data from a database.

roundrobin_partitioning.name: Round Robin Partitioning
roundrobin_partitioning.definition: A method of partitioning data where tuples are distributed evenly among partitions.

large_relations.name: Large Relations
large_relations.definition: Relations that contain a significant amount of data, making partitioning beneficial.

small_relations.name: Small Relations
small_relations.definition: Relations that contain a small amount of data, making partitioning unnecessary.

medium_relations.name: Medium-Sized Relations
medium_relations.definition: Relations that contain an intermediate amount of data, which can be partitioned across some nodes but not all.

replication_protocols.name: Replication Protocols
replication_protocols.definition: Protocols that guarantee consistency despite node and network failures.

block_access.name: Block Access
block_access.definition: The process of bringing a block from disk into main memory.

mutex.name: Mutex

test_and_set_instruction.name: Test-and-Set Instruction
test_and_set_instruction.definition: An instruction used to acquire a mutex (latch) on the lock table.

compare_and_swap_instruction.name: Compare-and-Swap Instruction
compare_and_swap_instruction.definition: An instruction used to acquire a mutex (latch) on the lock table.

phone_entity_set.name: Phone Entity Set
phone_entity_set.definition: A set of phones with attributes phone_number and location.

inst_phone_relationship_set.name: Inst_Phone Relationship Set
inst_phone_relationship_set.definition: A relationship set denoting the association between instructors and their phones.

snapshot_read.name: Snapshot Read
snapshot_read.definition: A process where a consistent scan of a relation is obtained using a snapshot timestamp.

buffer_management_approach_1.name: Buffer Management Approach 1
buffer_management_approach_1.definition: The database system reserves part of main memory to serve as a buffer that it, rather than the operating system, manages.

buffer_management_approach_2.name: Buffer Management Approach 2
buffer_management_approach_2.definition: The database system implements its buffer within the virtual memory provided by the operating system.

force_output.name: Force-Output
force_output.definition: The process of writing buffer blocks to disk.

database_buffer_manager.name: Database Buffer Manager
database_buffer_manager.definition: A component that allows processes to get shared and exclusive locks on the buffer.

http.name: HTTP

cgi_standard.definition: Defines how the web server communicates with application programs.

three_layer_architecture.definition: A web application architecture with a web server, an application server, and a database server.

two_layer_architecture.name: Two-Layer Web Application Architecture

throughput_numbers.name: Throughput Numbers

buffer_in_main_memory.name: Buffer in Main Memory
buffer_in_main_memory.definition: A component whose size affects the cost of all the algorithms considered.

effective_cache_size.name: Effective Cache Size

relation_instance.name: relation instance
relation_instance.definition: A specific instance of a relation, containing a specific set of rows.

read_committed_isolation_level.name: Read Committed Isolation Level
read_committed_isolation_level.definition: A weaker level of consistency where the query results are not guaranteed to be consistent.

hive_on_tez.name: Hive on Tez

online_analytic_processing_olap.definition: A system that allows a data analyst to look at different cross-tabs on the same data by interactively selecting the attributes in the cross-tab.

sorted_tree.name: Sorted Tree Structure

phantom_data.name: Phantom Data

undo_transaction.name: Undo Transaction

validation_based_protocol.name: Validation-Based Protocol
validation_based_protocol.definition: A protocol also known as the optimistic concurrency control protocol.

validation_timestamp.name: Validation Timestamp
validation_timestamp.definition: The validation timestamp, TS(Ti), which is used as the serialization order.

finish_timestamp.name: Finish Timestamp

lock_timeout.name: Lock Timeout

transaction_timeout.name: Transaction Timeout

short_transaction.name: Short Transaction

However, the execution is not serializable; the resultant database state cannot be obtained by any serial execution of the two transactions.
SQL Server offers the option of allowing some transactions to run under snapshot isolation, while allowing others to run under the serializable isolation level.

The problem with snapshot isolation is that, paradoxically, it provides too much isolation. Consider two transactions T and T′. In a serializable execution, either T sees all the updates made by T′ or T′ sees all the updates made by T, because one must follow the other in the serialization order. Under snapshot isolation, there are cases where neither transaction sees the updates of the other.

Stated simply, two-phase locking requires a transaction to have two phases, one where it acquires locks but does not release any, and a second phase where the transaction releases locks but does not acquire any.
In Chapter 18, we present the two-phase locking protocol, a simple, widely used technique that ensures serializability.
This protocol requires that each transaction issue lock and unlock requests in two phases: 1. Growing phase. A transaction may obtain locks, but may not release any lock.
2. Shrinking phase. A transaction may release locks, but may not obtain any new locks.
The point in the schedule where the transaction has obtained its final lock (the end of its growing phase) is called the lock point of the transaction.

A lookup on a B + -tree requires traversal of a path from the root of the tree to some leaf node. In contrast, it is sometimes possible to find the desired value in a B-tree before reaching a leaf node.

However, roughly n times as many keys are stored in the leaf level of a B-tree as in the nonleaf levels, and, since n is typically large, the benefit of finding certain values early is relatively small.

Moreover, the fact that fewer search keys appear in a nonleaf B-tree node, compared to B + -trees, implies that a B-tree has a smaller fanout and therefore may have depth greater than that of the corresponding B + -tree.
The primary distinction between the two approaches is that a B-tree eliminates the redundant storage of search-key values.

chunks.chunk_0000: The earliest database systems arose in the 1960s in response to the computerized management of commercial data. Those earlier applications were relatively simple compared to modern database applications. Modern applications include highly sophisticated, worldwide enterprises. All database applications, old and new, share important common elements. The central aspect of the application is not a program performing some calculation, but rather the data themselves. Today, some of the most valuable corporations are valuable not because of their physical assets, but rather because of the information they own. Imagine a bank without its data on accounts and customers or a social-network site that loses the connections among its users. Such companies' value would be almost totally lost under such circumstances. Database systems are used to manage collections of data that: - are highly valuable, - are relatively large, and - are accessed by multiple users and applications, often at the same time. The first database applications had only simple, precisely formatted, structured data. T oday, database applications may include data with complex relationships and a more  variable structure. As an example of an application with structured data, consider a university's records regarding courses, students, and course registration. The university keeps the same type of information about each course: course-identifier, title, department, course number, etc., and similarly for students: student-identifier, name, address, phone, etc. Course registration is a collection of pairs: one course identifier and one student identifier. Information of this sort has a standard, repeating structure and is representative of the type of database applications that go back to the 1960s. Contrast this simple university database application with a social-networking site
chunks.chunk_0001: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.1 Database-System Applications Content: . Contrast this simple university database application with a social-networking site. Users of the site post varying types of information about themselves ranging from simple items such as name or date of birth, to complex posts consisting of text, images, videos, and links to other users. There is only a limited amount of common structure among these data. Both of these applications, however, share the basic features of a database. Modern database systems exploit commonalities in the structure of data to gain efficiency but also allow for weakly structured data and for data whose formats are highly variable. As a result, a database system is a large, complex software system whose task is to manage a large, complex collection of data. Managing complexity is challenging, not only in the management of data but in any domain. Key to the management of complexity is the concept of abstraction . Abstraction allows a person to use a complex device or system without having to know the details of how that device or system is constructed. A person is able, for example, to drive a car by knowing how to operate its controls. However, the driver does not need to know how the motor was built nor how it operates. All the driver needs to know is an abstraction of what the motor does. Similarly, for a large, complex collection of data, a database system provides a simpler, abstract view of the information so that users and application programmers do not need to be aware of the underlying details of how data are stored and organized. By providing a high level of abstraction, a database system makes it possible for an enterprise to combine data of various types into a unified repository of the information needed to run the enterprise.  Here are some representative applications: ## Enterprise Information - Sales: For customer, product, and purchase - Page 3 information. - Accounting: For payments, receipts, account balances, assets, and other accounting information
chunks.chunk_0002: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.1 Database-System Applications Content: . - Accounting: For payments, receipts, account balances, assets, and other accounting information. - Human resources: For information about employees, salaries, payroll taxes, and benefits, and for generation of paychecks. - Manufacturing: For management of the supply chain and for tracking production of items in factories, inventories of items in warehouses and stores, and orders for items. - Banking and Finance - Banking: For customer information, accounts, loans, and banking transactions. - Credit card transactions: For purchases on credit cards and generation of monthly statements. - Finance: For storing information about holdings, sales, and purchases of financial instruments such as stocks and bonds; also for storing real-time market data to enable online trading by customers and automated trading by the firm. - Universities: For student information, course registrations, and grades (in addition to standard  - enterprise information such as human resources and accounting). - Airlines: For reservations and schedule information. Airlines were among the first to use databases in a geographically distributed manner. - Telecommunication: For keeping records of calls, texts, and data usage, generating monthly bills, maintaining balances on prepaid calling cards, and storing information about the communication networks. - Web-based services - Social-media: For keeping records of users, connections between users (such as friend/follows information), posts made by users, rating/like information about posts, etc. - Online retailers: For keeping records of sales data and orders as for any retailer, but also for tracking a user's product views, search terms, etc., for the purpose of identifying the best items to recommend to that user. - Online advertisements: For keeping records of click history to enable targeted advertisements, product suggestions, news articles, etc
chunks.chunk_0003: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.1 Database-System Applications Content: . - Online advertisements: For keeping records of click history to enable targeted advertisements, product suggestions, news articles, etc. People access such databases every time they do a web search, make an online purchase, or access a socialnetworking site. - Document databases: For maintaining collections of new articles, patents, published research papers, etc. - Navigation systems: For maintaining the locations of varies places of interest along with the exact routes of roads, train systems, buses, etc. Page 4 As this list illustrates, databases form an essential part not only of every enterprise but also of a large part of a person's daily activities.  The ways in which people interact with databases has changed over time. Early databases were maintained as back-office systems with which users interacted via printed reports and paper forms for input. As database systems became more sophisticated, better languages were developed for programmers to use in interacting with the data, along with user interfaces that allowed end users within the enterprise to query and update data. As the support for programmer interaction with databases improved, and computer hardware performance increased even as hardware costs decreased, more sophisticated applications emerged that brought database data into more direct contact not only with end users within an enterprise but also with the general public. Whereas once bank customers had to interact with a teller for every transaction, automated-teller machines (ATMs) allowed direct customer interaction. T oday, virtually every enterprise employs web applications or mobile applications to allow its customers to interact directly with the enterprise's database, and, thus, with the enterprise itself. The user, or customer, can focus on the product or service without being aware of the details of the large database that makes the interaction possible
chunks.chunk_0004: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.1 Database-System Applications Content: . The user, or customer, can focus on the product or service without being aware of the details of the large database that makes the interaction possible. For instance, when you read a social-media post, or access an online bookstore and browse a book or music collection, you are accessing data stored in a database. When you enter an order online, your order is stored in a database. When you access a bank web site and retrieve your bank balance and transaction information, the information is retrieved from the bank's database system. When you access a web site, information about you may be retrieved from a database to select which advertisements you should see. Almost every interaction with a smartphone results in some sort of database access. Furthermore, data about your web accesses may be stored in a database.  Thus, although user interfaces hide details of access to a database, and most people are not even aware they are dealing with a database, accessing databases forms an essential part of almost everyone's life today. Broadly speaking, there are two modes in which databases are used. - The first mode is to support online transaction processing , where a large number of users use the database, with each user retrieving relatively small amounts of data, and performing small updates. This is the primary mode of use for the vast majority of users of database applications such as those that we outlined earlier. - The second mode is to support data analytics , that is, the processing of data to draw conclusions, and infer rules or decision procedures, which are then used to drive business decisions. Page 5 For example, banks need to decide whether to give a loan to a loan applicant, online advertisers need to decide which advertisement to show to a particular user. These tasks are addressed in two steps. First, data-analysis techniques attempt to automatically discover rules and patterns from data and create predictive models
chunks.chunk_0005: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.1 Database-System Applications Content: . These tasks are addressed in two steps. First, data-analysis techniques attempt to automatically discover rules and patterns from data and create predictive models . These models take as input attributes ('features') of individuals, and output predictions such as likelihood of paying back a loan, or clicking on an advertisement, which are then used to make the business decision. As another example, manufacturers and retailers need to make decisions on what items to manufacture or order in what quantities; these decisions are driven significantly by techniques for analyzing past data, and predicting trends. The cost of making wrong decisions can be very high, and organizations are therefore willing to invest a lot of money to gather or purchase required data, and build systems that can use the data to make accurate predictions.  The field of data mining combines knowledge-discovery techniques invented by artificial intelligence researchers and statistical analysts with efficient implementation techniques that enable them to be used on extremely large databases.
chunks.chunk_0006: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.2 Purpose of Database Systems Content: To understand the purpose of database systems, consider part of a university organization that, among other data, keeps information about all instructors, students, departments, and course offerings. One way to keep the information on a computer is to store it in operating-system files. T o allow users to manipulate the information, the system has a number of application programs that manipulate the files, including programs to: - Add new students, instructors, and courses. - Register students for courses and generate class rosters. - Assign grades to students, compute grade point averages (GPA), and generate transcripts. Programmers develop these application programs to meet the needs of the university. New application programs are added to the system as the need arises. For example, suppose that a university decides to create a new major. As a result, the university creates a new department and creates new permanent files (or adds information to existing files) to record information about all the instructors in the department, students in that major, course offerings, degree requirements, and so on. The university may have to write new application programs to deal with rules specific to the new major. New application programs may also have to be written to handle new rules in the university. Thus, as time goes by, the system acquires more files and more application programs. This typical file-processing system is supported by a conventional operating system. The system stores permanent records in various files, and it needs different application programs to extract records from, and add records to, the appropriate files. Keeping organizational information in a file-processing system has a number of major disadvantages:  - Page 6 Data redundancy and inconsistency
chunks.chunk_0007: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.2 Purpose of Database Systems Content: . Keeping organizational information in a file-processing system has a number of major disadvantages:  - Page 6 Data redundancy and inconsistency. Since different programmers create the files and application programs over a long period, the various files are likely to have different structures, and the programs may be written in several programming languages. Moreover, the same information may be duplicated in several places (files). For example, if a student has a double major (say, music and mathematics), the address and telephone number of that student may appear in a file that consists of student records of students in the Music department and in a file that consists of student records of students in the Mathematics department. This redundancy leads to higher storage and access cost. In addition, it may lead to data inconsistency ; that is, the various copies of the same data may no longer agree. For example, a changed student address may be reflected in the Music department records but not elsewhere in the system. - Difficulty in accessing data. Suppose that one of the university clerks needs to find out the names of all students who live within a particular postal-code area. The clerk asks the data-processing department to generate such a list. Because the designers of the original system did not anticipate this request, there is no application program on hand to meet it. There is,  - however, an application program to generate the list of all students. The university clerk now has two choices: either obtain the list of all students and extract the needed information manually or ask a programmer to write the necessary application program. Both alternatives are obviously unsatisfactory. Suppose that such a program is written and that, several days later, the same clerk needs to trim that list to include only those students who have taken at least 60 credit hours. As expected, a program to generate such a list does not exist
chunks.chunk_0008: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.2 Purpose of Database Systems Content: . As expected, a program to generate such a list does not exist. Again, the clerk has the preceding two options, neither of which is satisfactory. The point here is that conventional file-processing environments do not allow needed data to be retrieved in a convenient and efficient manner. More responsive data-retrieval systems are required for general use. - Data isolation. Because data are scattered in various files, and files may be in different formats, writing new application programs to retrieve the appropriate data is difficult. - Integrity problems. The data values stored in the database must satisfy certain types of consistency constraints . Suppose the university maintains an account for each department, and records the balance amount in each account. Suppose also that the university requires that the account balance of a department may never fall below zero. Developers enforce these constraints in the system by adding appropriate code in the various application programs. However, when new constraints are added, it is difficult to change the programs to enforce them. The problem is compounded when constraints involve several data items from different files. - Atomicity problems. A computer system, like any other device, is subject to failure. In many applications,  - Page 7 it is crucial that, if a failure occurs, the data be restored to the consistent state that existed prior to the failure. Consider a banking system with a program to transfer $500 from account A to account B . If a system failure occurs during the execution of the program, it is possible that the $500 was removed from the balance of account A but was not credited to the balance of account B , resulting in an inconsistent database state. Clearly, it is essential to database consistency that either both the credit and debit occur, or that neither occur. That is, the funds transfer must be atomic -it must happen in its entirety or not at all
chunks.chunk_0009: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.2 Purpose of Database Systems Content: . That is, the funds transfer must be atomic -it must happen in its entirety or not at all. It is difficult to ensure atomicity in a conventional fileprocessing system. - Concurrent-access anomalies. For the sake of overall performance of the system and faster response, many systems allow multiple users to update the data simultaneously. Indeed, today, the largest internet retailers may have millions of accesses per day to their data by shoppers. In such an environment, interaction of concurrent updates is possible and may result in inconsistent data. Consider account A , with a balance of $10,000. If two bank clerks debit the account balance (by say $500 and $100, respectively) of account A at almost exactly the same time, the result of the concurrent executions may leave the account balance in an incorrect (or inconsistent) state. Suppose that the programs executing on behalf of each withdrawal read the old balance, reduce that value by the amount being withdrawn, and write the result back. If the two programs run concurrently, they may both read the value $10,000, and write back $9500 and $9900, respectively. Depending on which one writes the value last, the balance of account A may contain either $9500 or $9900, rather than the correct value of $9400. T o  - guard against this possibility, the system must maintain some form of supervision. But supervision is difficult to provide because data may be accessed by many different application programs that have not been coordinated previously. - As another example, suppose a registration program maintains a count of students registered for a course in order to enforce limits on the number of students registered. When a student registers, the program reads the current count for the courses, verifies that the count is not already at the limit, adds one to the count, and stores the count back in the database. Suppose two students register concurrently, with the count at 39
chunks.chunk_0010: Description: Chapter 1 Section 1.2 Purpose of Database Systems Content: . Suppose two students register concurrently, with the count at 39. The two program executions may both read the value 39, and both would then write back 40, leading to an incorrect increase of only 1, even though two students successfully registered for the course and the count should be 41. Furthermore, suppose the course registration limit was 40; in the above case both students would be able to register, leading to a violation of the limit of 40 students. - Security problems. Not every user of the database system should be able to access all the data. For example, in a university, payroll personnel need to see only that part of the database that has financial information. They do not need access to information about academic records. But since application programs are added to the file-processing system in an ad hoc manner, enforcing such security constraints is difficult. Page 8 These difficulties, among others, prompted both the initial development of database systems and the transition of file-based applications to database systems, back in the 1960s and 1970s.
